1. Market Overview & Long-Term Price Trend

The all-time high in this dataset stands at $5,377.30 recorded on March 03, 2026.

2. Volatility Analysis & Regime Detection

Volatility regime detection is performed using the 63-day (quarterly) rolling annualized standard deviation of log returns. Four regimes are defined by percentile thresholds:

Regime Definitions: Low (≤ P25 = 12.8%) • Normal (P25–P75 = 12.8%–18.5%) • High (P75–P95 = 18.5%–29.8%) • Crisis (> P95 = 29.8%)

3. Seasonal & Calendar-Based Patterns

Seasonal effects are assessed by aggregating daily returns to monthly and day-of-week buckets, then testing whether observed mean returns are statistically different from zero using t-tests and whether cross-group differences are significant using Kruskal-Wallis (monthly) and one-way ANOVA (day-of-week).

Omnibus Tests: Kruskal-Wallis test for monthly return differences: H = 10.00, p = 0.5306 — not statistically significant at 5%.
One-way ANOVA for day-of-week differences: F = 0.79, p = 0.5342 — not statistically significant at 5%.

4. Return Distribution & Tail Risk

The daily return distribution departs significantly from normality, exhibiting the fat tails and slight asymmetry characteristic of financial asset returns. This has direct implications for risk modeling and position sizing.

Normality Tests: Jarque-Bera: JB = 11459.3, p = 0.00e+00 — Shapiro-Wilk: W = 0.9393, p = 3.44e-41. Both tests decisively reject the null hypothesis of normality, confirming that standard Gaussian risk models significantly underestimate tail exposure. Excess kurtosis of 6.53 (vs. 0 for normal) indicates tail events are far more frequent than a bell curve would predict.

6. Key Takeaways & Forward-Looking Considerations

Current State (Mar 2026): Gold at $5,377.30 • Volatility regime: Crisis (36.5% annualized) • RSI: 66.6 • Trend: Bullish (vs 200 SMA)

Structural Findings

  1. Long-term uptrend with high volatility: A 12.38% CAGR over 26 years — competitive with equities — but at 17.7% annualized volatility, producing a Sharpe-like ratio of 0.70. The risk-adjusted return profile favors gold as a diversifier, not a core holding.
  2. Regime-dependent behavior is pronounced: Crisis regimes, while comprising only ~5% of days, generate outsized price swings. Low-volatility regimes tend to coincide with steady directional trends, making them favorable for carry and trend-following strategies.
  3. Fat tails demand non-Gaussian risk management: Excess kurtosis of 6.5 and a VaR(99%) of -3.05% daily confirm that standard normal assumptions underestimate tail risk by a wide margin. CVaR or Expected Shortfall should replace VaR in any risk framework applied to gold positions.
  4. Seasonal edges are statistically weak: The Kruskal-Wallis test for monthly differences does not show significance (p=0.5306), and day-of-week effects are absent (ANOVA p=0.5342). Observed monthly differences are largely noise and should not anchor allocation timing.
  5. Momentum signals have historically been informative: Gold has spent 70% of its history above the 200-day SMA, and SMA crossover transitions have generally aligned with sustained trend changes. RSI extremes (>70 or <30) have been infrequent (27.1% of days), suggesting gold rarely stays overbought or oversold for extended periods.

Implications for Portfolio Construction

  • Sizing: Given the -44.4% max drawdown, unconstrained gold allocations can introduce significant portfolio volatility. A 5-15% allocation captures diversification benefits without dominating portfolio risk.
  • Regime awareness: Volatility regime detection (even using simple rolling-window thresholds) can meaningfully inform position sizing: reduce in crisis regimes, lean into low-vol trending environments.
  • Risk modeling: Replace normal-distribution VaR with historical simulation or EVT-based approaches. The 6.5 excess kurtosis demands it.
  • Rebalancing: The absence of strong seasonal patterns means rebalancing should be driven by volatility and regime shifts rather than calendar rules.

Forward Scenarios

With gold currently in a crisis-volatility regime and trading above its 200-day moving average at an RSI of 66.6, the near-term technical setup suggests continued trend momentum, though elevated RSI warrants monitoring for potential mean-reversion. Key risk scenarios include a shift to crisis-level volatility (historically triggered by macro shocks), which would increase daily ranges by 210% relative to the low-vol baseline.
